summary: We built Anchor to help people understand why and how satellite fire counts change from year to year. Satellites pass over different places at different times, so the counts depend on both how many fires happen and when a satellite is there to detect them. Anchor has NASA's fire data on a calendar so you can compare what different satellites have detected year on year and in different regions. It highlights the years that are worth a look and shows the data behind each of the comparisons as well as the limitations of each comparison. For example, you can compare Brazil's official Amazon fire counts against a benchmark from another satellite. Anchor is designed to help researchers, reporters, and communities ask better questions before drawing conclusions from changing fire counts.
details: The official fire count in Brazil comes from one single satellite of NASA, namely Aqua, but its orbit has been shifting recently. The satellite used to scan the Amazon at about 1:37 pm but now does this around 3:00 pm. Fires behave differently throughout a day; hence, a shifted time leads to counting another amount of fires regardless of any changes in the landscape. This web site represents Anchor – a platform where we measure the extent of this problem. Since the orbit of VIIRS satellites didn't shift, their fire counts were used in order to calculate what Aqua would've counted if it hadn't. In 2025, Aqua counted 43,002 fires in the Amazon, while our estimation gave 33,172.We examined whether there was a role played by clouds or a shift in the viewing angle of the satellite, but none of those explained the discrepancy, and most of it is explained by the later pass. The other satellite, the twin of Aqua, called Terra, moved towards earlier times of day and saw fewer fires, and that would be expected if timing is the key. We have a fire calendar by month in six regions going back to 2002, and also a map where clicking on the fire will give information about which satellite observed it and when. The Aqua satellite is near the end of its life, so we demonstrated that NOAA-20 gives the same results.Our analysis was performed using Python, while the site itself is made using React. The information we use comes from NASA FIRMS, NOAA GOES-East satellite, and Brazil’s national space research institute INPE. Our figures differ from the INPE official figures by less than 10% in 96.6% of cases, and every figure on the site includes its uncertainty range.
